motion: Progress towards democracy has halted in the Arab world.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: How can you claim democratic progress continues when citizens cannot reliably replace rulers, restrain force, or obtain impartial justice? What concrete change in governing power would distinguish your gradual progress from a system that has simply stopped?

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: Your test is too narrow: democratic progress can begin with citizens gaining voice before they gain full control. That continuing voice is the point you overlook, so your conclusion does not follow.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Even if discussion survives, citizens still lack the power to make rulers obey. That gap between demands and decisions is the clearest sign that democracy has halted.

turns.text: You say the ballot is decoration, but that ignores citizens using elections, campaigns, and public pressure to widen their choices. Even restricted institutions can become openings for reform, so your example shows unfinished democracy, not a complete halt.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant that public pressure can create openings. But an opening is not progress if authorities close it whenever citizens threaten their control. The central question is whether people gain governing power, and repeated closure shows democratic progress has halted.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I reject the premise that closure erases every gain. Citizens who return, organize, and demand rights after repression are building political capacity. If power must constantly answer those demands, however imperfectly, democracy is advancing rather than standing still.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If this is genuine progress, what meaningful power can ordinary citizens use to remove leaders who ignore them, challenge security institutions, and secure independent courts? Without those safeguards, why call pressure democratic progress instead of resistance to a halted system?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your question treats progress as something visible only after a complete transformation. I am answering the broader point: citizens can expand rights, expectations, and participation before institutions fully change. That gradual expansion is precisely why the motion is false.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A community may fill streets demanding civilian rule, only to see the same power holders write the rules, limit parties, and punish dissent. Their courage matters, but the unchanged authority proves the democratic path has halted, not advanced.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The related issue is whether courage survives repression, and it often does through families, unions, local groups, and public discussion. Those networks are not full democracy, but they preserve demands and create foundations. So progress has not halted.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I agree that networks can preserve demands. But preserving a demand is different from achieving accountable rule; if each opening ends with the same authorities stronger and citizens less protected, the outcome is stagnation. The motion describes that political reality.
